subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
subtype: Laws as agreements that serve people [Actor]
passage:
At eleven at night the tap in Tarun's rented room in Hadapsar coughed once and went dry again. Downstairs, Anand was already holding a spanner. "The main line runs right under our lane. One small cut, a pipe to our tank, done. Half the next colony does it."
Tarun, a second-year civil engineering student, looked at the pipe. He had spent a whole term on pressure drops. "The water rule isn't there to annoy us. It's how a whole ward agrees to share one pipe. If we cut in, Mrs Kamble's taps downhill go dry instead of ours."
"So we just suffer the four a.m. slot forever?"
"No. The slot is unfair to everyone who works nights. The ward committee meets Saturday. I'll bring the timings, you bring signatures."
Anand put the spanner down, grumbling, and went to find a pen.

qa.q: When does the ward committee meet?
qa.a: The ward committee meets on Saturday.

qa.q: Why does Tarun think cutting into the main line is wrong, even though the water timing bothers him too?
qa.a: He sees the water rule as the ward's shared agreement for one pipe, and he knows a cut would leave Mrs Kamble's taps downhill dry instead.

qa.q: What choice does Tarun make at the turning point, and why might it work better than the spanner?
qa.a: Instead of cutting in or putting up with the four a.m. slot, he takes timings and signatures to the ward committee, which can change the slot for everyone, including night workers.

qa.q: How would Mrs Kamble's household be affected if Anand had used the spanner that night?
qa.a: Her taps would lose pressure and could go dry, so the lane's problem would simply be pushed downhill onto her without anyone asking her.

grounding: A student treats a water rule as a shared agreement that protects everyone, refuses to break it, and takes its unfair timing to the ward committee.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
subtype: Laws as agreements that serve people [Actor]
passage:
"Mummy, did you see the notice? Cycle rickshaws are banned from Station Road from next month."
"Good," said Mummy, ladling dal. "Law is law. That road is a mess."
Tarun Kaka snorted. "Law! Old Shinde should just ride there anyway. Who stops an old man?"
Nilesh, in his second year of law college, put his roti down. "The traffic police will, Kaka, and they'd be right to fine him. Road rules exist so nobody gets run over. That part is fair."
"Then what's your problem?" Papa asked.
"Nobody asked Shinde or the other riders. Half his fares are on that road. A rule that takes someone's living without hearing him isn't finished yet."
"So?"
"The ward's objection window is open till Friday. I'll write it with him tonight, and the riders' union can speak at the hearing."
Tarun Kaka shrugged. "And if they still say no?"
"Then we go to the next council meeting. Not through the police barricade."

qa.q: What does the notice ban from Station Road?
qa.a: Cycle rickshaws are banned from Station Road from next month.

qa.q: What does Nilesh think is wrong with the new rule, even though he agrees road rules are fair?
qa.a: He thinks a rule that takes away Shinde's living without hearing him or the other riders isn't finished yet.

qa.q: When Tarun Kaka asks what happens if they still say no, what does Nilesh's reply show about his choice?
qa.a: It shows he will keep working through hearings and the council rather than breaking the rule, even if the first objection fails.

qa.q: How might Shinde feel about Nilesh helping with the objection instead of being told to ride there anyway?
qa.a: He would likely feel his living is taken seriously and that he has a real voice at the hearing, without risking a fine or his safety on a busy road.

grounding: A law student at the family dinner table argues that road rules protect people but that an unfair ban should be challenged through the objection process, not ignored or simply obeyed.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
passage:
For three winters Ira had written the same fine in the same notebook: anyone caught carrying wood out of the reserve above Lingthem paid it, neighbours included. She believed in the rule; the slope had slid twice where trees were cut.
This January the road closed under snow and the gas cylinders stopped coming. On her rounds Ira found old Pema beside a cold stove, two grandchildren wrapped in one blanket.
She did not look away, and she did not quietly let people take wood either. That night she wrote a formal objection to the range office asking for a fallen-wood permit for every household until the road opened, and read it aloud at the forest committee.
The committee voted: permits only for homes with elders or infants. Ira had asked for more. She pinned the result on the panchayat board, issued Pema's permit first, and went back to writing fines for everyone else.

qa.q: Which homes did the committee vote to give permits to?
qa.a: Permits went only to homes with elders or infants.

qa.q: How can you tell Ira still believes in the wood rule while she objects to it?
qa.a: She keeps fining even neighbours and remembers the slope sliding where trees were cut, so her objection is about harm in the snow, not about the rule itself.

qa.q: At the turning point beside Pema's cold stove, what choice did Ira make instead of quietly letting people take wood?
qa.a: She wrote a formal objection to the range office and read it aloud at the forest committee, so the change was decided openly.

qa.q: How might a family without elders or infants see the committee's decision?
qa.a: They might feel left out in the cold, but because the vote was open and the result pinned on the board, they could see how and why it was decided.

grounding: A forest guard enforces the wood rule in ordinary times, objects formally when snow makes it harmful, and accepts a committee decision narrower than she asked for.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
passage:
Lindiwe had processed housing forms at the Durban municipal office for two years, and she sent back every one without an original ID. Copies were easy to fake, and a fake had once cost a real family its flat.
Then Sami came in, seventy-one, smelling faintly of smoke. His room had burned on Tuesday, papers and all. The rule said no original, no place on the list, and a replacement ID could take months.
That afternoon Lindiwe filed an exception request with the review panel, attaching a fire report and a letter from Sami's street committee. She asked that fire victims keep their queue place with a sworn statement.
The panel refused the general change but agreed Sami's case could be paused, not dropped. Lindiwe felt the sting of losing. She phoned Sami herself, explained the panel's reasons, and booked him the next slot at the home affairs office.

qa.q: What did Lindiwe attach to her exception request?
qa.a: She attached a fire report and a letter from Sami's street committee.

qa.q: What was Lindiwe feeling when the panel refused the general change?
qa.a: She felt the sting of losing, because she had asked for all fire victims to keep their place, yet she still respected the panel's decision.

qa.q: What choice did Lindiwe make after the ruling went against her, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She accepted it, phoned Sami herself with the reasons and booked his ID appointment, so he was neither confused nor dropped from the list.

qa.q: How might Sami see the office differently because Lindiwe raised the request instead of just returning his form?
qa.a: He might feel the office treated him as a person who had lost everything, not just a missing document, even though his case was only paused.

grounding: A housing officer keeps the ID rule in ordinary cases, raises a formal exception when a fire victim would be harmed, and accepts the panel's partial refusal.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
subtype: Person affected by a fair process feels respected [Receiver]
passage:
Subject: Thank you for Thursday

Dear Sudha ma'am,

I wanted to write before the weekend. When I filed my complaint about the unpaid overtime for the March server shift, I honestly expected a two-line reply from the system. Instead you called me into the review, let me explain the night we moved the whole billing platform, and read the pre-approval policy aloud to all of us.

You also said why it exists: last year two teams billed hours nobody had asked for. I still think my case was different, and the panel still said no. That stung a little.

But you wrote down every point I made, and your letter answered each one with a reason. Nobody here has done that for me before. Next time I'll get approval first, and if something seems wrong, I'll raise it again, knowing it will be heard.

Regards,
Mohit

qa.q: What did Sudha read aloud during the review?
qa.a: She read the pre-approval policy aloud to all of them.

qa.q: How does Mohit feel about losing the complaint, and what shows it?
qa.a: Mohit says it stung a little and still thinks the case was different, yet feels respected because every point was written down and answered with a reason.

qa.q: Which moment in the review turned Mohit's expectation around?
qa.a: Being called in to explain the night of the billing move, instead of getting a two-line reply, showed Mohit the complaint was really being weighed.

qa.q: What might Sudha gain by answering each of Mohit's points with a reason, even while saying no?
qa.a: She gains an employee who trusts the process and will follow the approval rule next time instead of feeling brushed aside.

grounding: An employee whose overtime complaint was heard openly and answered point by point feels respected despite losing and trusts the process more.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
subtype: Person affected by a fair process feels respected [Receiver]
passage:
You want to know why I stopped grumbling about the depot, Ujjwal? Pour the tea, and I'll tell you.
Last winter they moved me to the late routes, the ones that end near midnight. I'm Parveen, twenty-five, a conductor for six years, and I was furious. Three people with less service kept their day shifts. My husband said I'd get nowhere, but I wrote a complaint anyway.
I thought it would sit in a drawer. Instead the depot manager called a hearing. My union rep came, the three conductors came, and she put the seniority list on the table for all of us. Two of them had medical duty limits I hadn't known about. The third had asked first, in writing.
She said no to me. Then she gave me the date of the next rota review and put my name first for day routes.
I went home tired. But I trusted that office for the first time.

qa.q: What did the depot manager put on the table at the hearing?
qa.a: She put the seniority list on the table for all of them.

qa.q: What did Parveen expect would happen to the complaint, and how did that change?
qa.a: She thought it would sit in a drawer, but after the open hearing and the reasons, she trusted the office for the first time.

qa.q: Which part of the hearing was the turning point for Parveen?
qa.a: Seeing the seniority list and learning why the others kept day shifts turned her anger into understanding, even though the answer was no.

qa.q: If you were Ujjwal hearing this story, what might you take from it about raising a complaint?
qa.a: That a complaint is worth filing where people listen openly, because even a no can come with fairness and a clear next step.

grounding: A bus conductor whose complaint gets an open hearing and a reasoned refusal feels respected and comes to trust the depot.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
passage:
Monday. The notice by the hotel kitchen's time clock said tips would now go only to waiters. Shankar, a line cook, expected Lokesh to explode; Lokesh had worked the tandoor for four years. Instead he read it twice, took a photo and went back to his skewers. He's scared, Shankar decided.
Thursday. At the staff council, Lokesh stood up with a typed page: the cooks' hours on banquet nights, and a request for a shared pool. When Venkat from the grill muttered that they should all slow down service to teach management a lesson, Lokesh shook his head. "I like this place. That's why I'm asking properly."
Three weeks later. The revised notice gave the kitchen a quarter share, less than Lokesh had asked for. Shankar watched him shake the manager's hand, and realised he had been wrong about which of them was scared.

qa.q: What share did the revised notice give the kitchen?
qa.a: The revised notice gave the kitchen a quarter share.

qa.q: What did Shankar first think Lokesh's quiet reaction meant, and why did that change?
qa.a: Shankar assumed Lokesh was scared, but the typed page and the calm refusal to slow down service showed that the quiet came from care for the place, not fear.

qa.q: When Venkat suggested slowing down service, what choice did Lokesh make, and why was it a turning point?
qa.a: He refused and stayed with the staff council, which kept trust with management and made a partial win possible.

qa.q: How might the hotel manager see Lokesh after the council, compared with a cook who slowed service in protest?
qa.a: The manager probably sees someone who cares about the hotel and can be reasoned with, which made the quarter share easier to agree to.

grounding: Over three weeks a cook watches a colleague challenge an unfair tip rule through the staff council without sabotage, and learns that loyalty and principle fit together.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
passage:
"Ritu, you keep saying people who complain at work are troublemakers. Let your Nani tell you about Joseph.
I was twenty-four, a clerk in the mill office in Coimbatore. One monsoon the bus drivers struck for a week, and the management passed an order: anyone who clocked in even ten minutes late lost the whole day's pay. Half of us walked six kilometres every morning.
Some clerks tore the notice down at night. Others paid and cursed. Joseph, who sat across from me, did neither. He kept coming on time, wrote to the works committee with the strike dates, and signed it in his own name. I was sure he'd be sacked.
He wasn't. The committee gave a half-hour grace on strike days. And Joseph still stayed late every Friday closing the accounts, same as before. That's when I understood a person can love a place and still tell it where it is wrong."

qa.q: What did the management order say about clocking in late?
qa.a: Anyone who clocked in even ten minutes late lost the whole day's pay.

qa.q: What did Nani expect would happen to Joseph after the letter, and what does that suggest about her view back then?
qa.a: She was sure he'd be sacked, which suggests she then saw objecting as risky and even disloyal.

qa.q: Which of Joseph's choices made the change possible, compared with the other clerks?
qa.a: He neither tore down the notice nor paid and cursed; he wrote to the works committee with dates and his own name, which the committee could act on.

qa.q: Why might Nani be telling Ritu this story now?
qa.a: Ritu calls people who complain at work troublemakers, and Nani wants Ritu to see that someone can object openly and still be loyal.

grounding: An elder recalls watching a colleague challenge an unfair late-pay order through the works committee while staying loyal, and what she learned from it.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
passage:
Shalini: Siami, did you see the vendors' group? Mrs Pachuau's son is furious
Lalremsiami: saw it. the lottery put her stall at the far end again
Shalini: she can't push her wheelchair up that slope with a crate on her lap 😟
Shalini: just give her the gate spot. you're the secretary
Lalremsiami: I can't hand it out alone. our constitution says stall rules change only by vote at the general meeting
Lalremsiami: but I can put it on Thursday's agenda
Shalini: people will call it favouritism
Lalremsiami: then we lay it out plainly. everyone has a right to a fair draw. she also has a right to reach her own stall
Lalremsiami: I'll ask her to speak first, then anyone who disagrees
Shalini: and if they vote no?
Lalremsiami: then I bring an amendment: one step-free spot kept out of the lottery, reviewed every year
Shalini: ok. I'll print the agenda 👍

qa.q: Where did the lottery put Mrs Pachuau's stall?
qa.a: The lottery put her stall at the far end again.

qa.q: Why does Lalremsiami refuse to simply give Mrs Pachuau the gate spot, and what does Lalremsiami want instead?
qa.a: Lalremsiami believes stall rules can only change by vote, and wants both the fair draw and Mrs Pachuau's access weighed openly at the meeting.

qa.q: What small step did Lalremsiami plan that could fix the rule for good?
qa.a: An amendment for one step-free spot kept out of the lottery and reviewed every year, so the fix is part of the rules, not a one-time favour.

qa.q: What would change for Mrs Pachuau by being invited to speak first at the meeting?
qa.a: She could explain the slope and the crate in her own words, so the other vendors hear the problem directly instead of as gossip about favouritism.

grounding: A market secretary facing a lottery rule that blocks a wheelchair user names the rights at stake, invites her to speak, follows the voting procedure and plans an amendment.

subtopic: Kohlberg social contract stage
passage:
The canal water in Rampura came by turns, one field after another through the week, and Kishore, twenty-six, kept the register for the water committee. This summer Gurleen's turn fell between one and four at night. Since her husband's death she farmed alone, and she had stopped going out at night after a pack of stray dogs chased her.
Some men told Kishore to quietly swap her turn. Others said a turn is a turn.
Kishore called the committee to the panchayat ghar on Sunday. He wrote two lines on the board: every field's fair share of water; every farmer's safety in getting it. Then he asked Gurleen to speak, and after her, Harbans, whose day turn would move.
The rules said any change needed two-thirds of members. They voted to let Harbans swap with her for one season. Kishore then proposed a standing swap list for anyone who cannot irrigate at night, to be voted on next month.

qa.q: What two lines did Kishore write on the board?
qa.a: Every field's fair share of water, and every farmer's safety in getting it.

qa.q: What might Gurleen have been worried about before the meeting?
qa.a: She was probably worried about going to her field alone at night after the dogs chased her, and perhaps that asking for a change would look like special treatment.

qa.q: When men told him to quietly swap her turn, what did Kishore choose, and why was it wiser?
qa.a: He called the committee and followed the two-thirds rule, so the change was agreed openly and Harbans had a say instead of being overruled.

qa.q: How is Harbans affected by the way the swap was decided?
qa.a: Harbans gives up a day turn for a season but was asked to speak and saw the vote, so the loss comes with a fair hearing rather than a quiet deal.

grounding: A water committee secretary handles a night-turn conflict by naming fairness and safety, inviting both affected farmers to speak, following the vote rule and proposing a better rule.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
"Dadi, Chintu hit me with the spoon!"
Urmila Dadi looked up from the peas. "And what did you do, Sumit?"
"Nothing. I didn't hit back." He puffed out his chest. "Hitting is bad."
"Why is it bad?"
"Because Mummy gets angry. And then no cartoons."
"What if Mummy is at the office?"
Sumit frowned hard. "Then... still bad. Still no cartoons. Later."
"And Chintu? He's only two."
"He'll get a big scolding when he's big," Sumit said, very sure. "That's the rule."
Dadi pulled him onto her lap. "Show me your arm. Does it hurt where the spoon went?"

qa.q: What did Chintu hit Sumit with?
qa.a: Chintu hit him with the spoon.

qa.q: Why does Sumit think hitting is bad?
qa.a: He thinks it is bad because Mummy gets angry and the cartoons stop, so right and wrong mean whether a grown-up will be cross.

qa.q: What could Dadi try next to help Sumit look beyond the scolding?
qa.a: Asking about his sore arm is a good start; she could gently link it to how the spoon hurt, so hitting is wrong because it hurts someone.

qa.q: How might Chintu, who is only two, understand the rule Sumit is so sure about?
qa.a: At two, Chintu probably has no idea there is a rule at all, so Sumit's certainty about a future scolding means nothing to him yet.

grounding: A five-year-old judges hitting wrong because Mummy gets angry and cartoons stop, treating the rule as a fixed fact.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
Nursery note, Tuesday. Written by Neelam, class teacher.
At water time Swati, four, saw Dev push Mahi off the bench. She ran to me first. "Dev did pushing! Now you will be angry?" I asked why pushing is wrong. She thought hard. "Because teacher gets angry. And no star." When I asked what if I hadn't seen, she looked puzzled, as if a rule simply is, like rain.
Later she checked my face before taking her turn on the slide.
Next step: at circle time I'll ask the children how Mahi felt, and read the story about the hurt rabbit. I mentioned it to her mother at pickup; this is very usual at four.

qa.q: What did Swati say would happen because of the pushing?
qa.a: She said the teacher gets angry and there would be no star.

qa.q: What does Swati's puzzled look suggest about how she sees rules?
qa.a: It suggests she feels a rule simply is, like rain, and hasn't thought that pushing could be wrong even if no teacher saw it.

qa.q: How could Neelam support Swati at circle time?
qa.a: By asking how Mahi felt and reading the hurt-rabbit story, Neelam can help Swati link pushing to someone getting hurt, not only to an angry teacher.

qa.q: How might Mahi feel if everyone only talked about the teacher being angry?
qa.a: Mahi might feel the fall itself was forgotten, since all the attention went to the rule and not to the one who got pushed. 🥺

grounding: A teacher's note records a four-year-old judging pushing wrong only because the teacher will be angry, treating the rule as a plain fact.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
Coach's note, 12 August. Written by Francis D'Souza, under-16 football.
Samir, fifteen, is the boy everyone wants on their side: first to set out cones, last to leave. This week the older boys planned to skip Saturday's practice to protest the new captain. When they asked Samir, I saw him look around the whole circle before he answered. "Okay. If everyone is."
Afterwards he stayed back, tying and untying one lace. "Coach, I don't want them to think I'm a traitor. But my father drives me here at six every day. He'll think I'm useless if I skip."
I asked what he thought a good teammate owed the new captain. He went quiet, then asked if I could just make Saturday compulsory, so the choice wouldn't be his.
Next: meet the captain and the older boys together on Monday, and give Samir a chance to speak for himself.

qa.q: Why did the older boys plan to skip Saturday's practice?
qa.a: They planned to skip it to protest the new captain.

qa.q: What was Samir worried about as he tied and untied his lace?
qa.a: He was worried the boys would think he was a traitor and that his father would think he was useless if he skipped.

qa.q: What went wrong when Samir asked for Saturday to be made compulsory, and what could help him instead?
qa.a: He tried to hand the choice to someone else so nobody could blame him; talking through what he owes the new captain could help him make and own a choice.

qa.q: How might the new captain feel if Samir skipped just to keep the older boys happy?
qa.a: The captain might feel alone and see Samir's easy friendliness as reserved for the popular side, which would make the team feel less safe.

grounding: A coach's note shows a fifteen-year-old torn between loyalty to his group and his father's approval, unable to face disappointing either.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
Thursday night
Ramesh called at nine. There's a concert at the city ground on Saturday and his parents said no. His plan: he tells them he's studying at my place, and if Aunty phones, I say yes, he's here.
I said "haan, obviously" before I'd even thought. That's what friends do. Ramesh covered for me at school twice. If I back out, the whole group will know by Monday, and I'll be the one who ditched.
But Aunty feeds me every time I go over. She calls me "the sensible one". And Mummy thinks Ramesh's family trusts both of us. I keep hearing Aunty's voice on the phone, and me lying into it.
I don't want to be a bad friend. I don't want to be a bad son either. Why does being good to one side mean letting down the other?
Can't sleep. Will talk to Ramesh at the bus stop.
Jatin

qa.q: What does Aunty call Jatin?
qa.a: She calls him the sensible one.

qa.q: Why did Jatin agree to Ramesh's plan so quickly?
qa.a: He wanted to be seen as a loyal friend, since Ramesh had covered for him twice, and he feared being called the one who ditched.

qa.q: What choice is Jatin facing at the bus stop, and what might help him make it?
qa.a: Whether to back out of the cover story; he could tell Ramesh honestly that he won't lie to Aunty but still stands by him as a friend.

qa.q: If Aunty found out about the plan, how might she feel about Jatin?
qa.a: She might feel let down by the boy she trusted as the sensible one, which is exactly the disappointment Jatin dreads. 😔

grounding: A teenager's diary shows him caught between being a loyal friend and a good son, finding it very hard to disappoint either side.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
The hostel rule was taped beside the register at the front desk: no visitors in the lobby after eight. At ten past eight, Tejas came in with his grandmother, grey with tiredness from a delayed train.
"Just till my cousin comes to take her," he said. "Forty minutes."
Vinita, twenty, the student desk volunteer that month, didn't even glance at the clock. "I'm sorry. After eight, no visitors."
"She's seventy-three. It's raining."
"If I let her sit, tomorrow everyone's aunt sits, and the day after nobody reads anything on that board. A rule only works if it works for everyone."
Tejas stared at her. His grandmother pulled her shawl tighter. "Come, beta, we'll wait at the tea stall."
Vinita watched them go, her hand flat on the rule sheet, and felt right and a little cold at the same time.

qa.q: What time did Tejas come in with his grandmother?
qa.a: He came in at ten past eight.

qa.q: What did Vinita feel as she watched them leave?
qa.a: She felt right and a little cold at the same time, sure the rule mattered yet uneasy about sending an old woman into the rain.

qa.q: Where was the turning point, and what choice could have kept order and still helped?
qa.a: When Tejas said his grandmother was seventy-three and it was raining; Vinita could have called the warden for a one-time exception noted in the register.

qa.q: How might Tejas see the hostel rules after that night?
qa.a: He may see them as rigid and uncaring, since they left his tired grandmother waiting at a tea stall in the rain.

grounding: A hostel desk volunteer enforces the visitor rule by asking what happens if everyone is let in, keeping order but being hard on a rare case.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
Dear Tenzin,
I know you're angry, and I'm writing because I couldn't say this properly in the union office.
When the river flooded your hostel block and your club's receipts went with it, I believed every word. I still do. But as treasurer I can't release the trek money without bills. The rule says no bill, no money, and I signed that I would keep it.
Think about it. If I pay you on trust, next month the dance club will have lost receipts, then the quiz club, and soon the union account is whatever anyone says it is. The rules are the only thing holding that money together for everybody.
I also know this is hard on you. You did nothing wrong. Maybe the shops can reprint the bills? I'll come with you if you want.
Your friend,
Nirmala

qa.q: What happened to the club's receipts?
qa.a: They went with the water when the river flooded Tenzin's hostel block.

qa.q: How can you tell Nirmala feels torn, not just strict?
qa.a: Nirmala says Tenzin did nothing wrong, admits the rule is hard on Tenzin, and offers to go to the shops together.

qa.q: What does Nirmala's pay-on-trust argument do well, and where does it fall short?
qa.a: It protects the union's money for every club, but it treats a real flood like any excuse and leaves Tenzin's trek at risk.

qa.q: What might it be like for Tenzin to read this letter after the argument?
qa.a: Tenzin may still feel stuck and angry about the trek, but perhaps less judged, since the letter says plainly that Tenzin is believed.

grounding: A student treasurer holds to the no-bill rule because rules keep order for everyone, while seeing that it is hard on a friend's rare flood case.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
subtype: Stages are tendencies, not labels on people [Observer]
passage:
"Vijay, you're new to tutoring, so let your Preeti Masi tell you about a mistake she nearly made. Sit.
Thirty years ago, in my second year of teaching, I had a student called Harish, nineteen. In class debates he'd say things like, 'Don't cheat, you'll get caught.' I had just read about moral stages, and I wrote in my register: Harish, early stage. Very clever of me.
Then the hostel mess dismissed the cook's helper for taking leftover rice home. Harish stood up in the student meeting and argued that a man feeding his children was not a thief and the rule should change, and he wrote the petition himself.
Same boy. Different day, different question, different reasoning.
I rubbed out my note. The stages help you see where thinking might grow next, Vijay. They are not a ladder for ranking who is good. Harish taught me that, not the book."

qa.q: What did Preeti write in her register about Harish?
qa.a: She wrote: Harish, early stage.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel about her register note once Harish argued for the helper?
qa.a: She felt her label had been hasty, even a bit foolish, which is why she mocks herself with 'very clever of me' and rubbed the note out.

qa.q: What choice at the turning point does Preeti want Vijay to learn from?
qa.a: Rubbing out the label and using stages to see where thinking can grow, instead of ranking students as better or worse people.

qa.q: How might Harish have been treated if Preeti had kept her note?
qa.a: He might have been seen as a shallow thinker in her class, and his fair argument about the helper could have been overlooked.

grounding: A teacher recalls seeing the same student reason at different levels in class and at a hostel meeting, and learning to use stages to see growth, not to rank people.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
subtype: Stages are tendencies, not labels on people [Observer]
passage:
Ten minutes into Arnab's evening ethics tutorial, the power went. Twelve phone torches came on, the fan died, and the room at the night college grew hot.
"Keep going, sir?"
"Keep going." He was twenty-two and had planned slides; now he had only a question. "A shopkeeper gives you too much change. Do you return it?"
Kalyani, nineteen, answered from the back. "Return it. He might notice, and then you're in trouble." Arnab caught himself reaching for his notebook to write a stage number beside her name.
Twenty minutes later, sweating in the dark, they argued about whether a factory should cut pay when the staff bus is late. Kalyani spoke again. "Rules should protect workers. If the bus is late for everyone, punishing them isn't fair. It's just easy."
Arnab closed the notebook. Same student, same hot evening, two kinds of reasoning. He had nearly graded a person on one sentence.

qa.q: What did Kalyani say about returning the extra change?
qa.a: She said to return it because he might notice, and then you're in trouble.

qa.q: Why did Arnab close his notebook?
qa.a: He realised he had nearly graded Kalyani on one sentence, when she had just reasoned about fairness in a very different way.

qa.q: What would you advise Arnab to do with the stage idea from now on?
qa.a: Use it to notice how a student's reasoning shifts between questions and where it could grow, not to write a number beside a name.

qa.q: What would change for Kalyani if the power cut had ended the class after the first question?
qa.a: Arnab might have kept a stage number beside her name, and her stronger point about unfair pay cuts would never have been heard.

grounding: A young tutor in a dark, hot classroom sees one student reason at two different levels and drops the idea of labelling her with a stage.

When Dolma's son was arrested in town, the village council in Kaza decided her family would not draw from the common tap until the case was over. "We don't want trouble here," the headman said. No one argued.
Sahil, twenty-five, taught at the village school. Next morning he walked with Dolma to the tap, filled her two cans, and carried one home for her. At the council he said, "Her grandson is in my class. He is not accused of anything. Nor is she. Water is not a reward for good behaviour."
The council fined him, and his landlord asked him to find another room. He paid, packed, and moved into a draughty storeroom behind the school.
He was no saint about it. At night he lay awake wondering whether his mother would be ashamed of the gossip, and whether he had been proud rather than right. In the morning he carried the cans again.

qa.q: What did the village council decide about Dolma's family?
qa.a: It decided her family would not draw from the common tap until the case was over.

qa.q: What was Sahil worried about at night, even while he kept carrying the cans?
qa.a: He worried his mother would be ashamed of the gossip, and whether he had been proud rather than right.

qa.q: What was Sahil's turning-point choice, and what did it cost him?
qa.a: He chose to fetch water with Dolma openly and tell the council why, and it cost him a fine and his room.

qa.q: How might Dolma's grandson see Sahil after this?
qa.a: He might see his teacher as someone who treated his family as people when the village turned away, and that could stay with him a long time. 🤍

grounding: A young teacher acts on his own principle of dignity against the village council's ban, accepts the fine and loss of his room, and still doubts himself.

The council notice on the park railings in Nairobi was new: no food handouts without a permit, and a fine for anyone who ignored it. The permit list had a two-year wait.
Wanjiru, twenty-six, had shared her lunch there with the same three street boys every Friday for a year. Her flatmate Mina read the notice aloud. "You'll get fined. People at your office already think you're mad."
"They're children, Mina. I'm not going to make them watch me eat."
On Friday an officer wrote her the fine. Wanjiru paid it that afternoon and that night wrote to her ward councillor asking for a simple permit for small, one-person sharing.
Mina teased her about being a saint. Wanjiru laughed. "Saints don't check their bank balance twice after a fine. Most days I follow rules just to stay out of trouble, like everyone."

qa.q: How long was the wait on the permit list?
qa.a: The permit list had a two-year wait.

qa.q: Why did Wanjiru keep sharing her lunch after the notice went up?
qa.a: She believed the boys were children who should not have to watch her eat, and that mattered more to her than the fine or her office's opinion.

qa.q: Besides paying the fine, what step did Wanjiru take, and why is it a sensible choice?
qa.a: She wrote to her ward councillor asking for a simple permit for small sharing, which works to change the rule rather than only defying it.

qa.q: How does Mina's view of Wanjiru's choice differ from Wanjiru's own?
qa.a: Mina sees risk and a reputation for being mad and jokes about sainthood, while Wanjiru sees an ordinary person who mostly follows rules but won't bend on this one.

grounding: A young woman acts on her principle of human dignity against a feeding by-law, accepts the fine, and admits that most days she follows rules like anyone.
